**Why OIG's own dashboard says 586**
OIG's dashboard (https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/data-dashboard) shows 586 open, 19 more than this data. A row-by-row check found the same recommendations in both. The extra 19 on OIG's side are blank rows on its pages. So it's fair to say "567 open (586 on OIG's dashboard, which includes 19 blank rows)."

**How old the open items are** (567 total, by publication year)

| Year | Open recommendations | Reports |
|---|---|---|
| 2026 | 369 | 103 |
| 2025 | 118 | 47 |
| 2024 | 24 | 14 |
| 2023 | 24 | 8 |
| 2022 | 13 | 7 |
| 2021 | 18 | 9 |

These report counts include only reports that have at least one open recommendation.

OIG's own age breakdown is 409 open under 1 year, 160 open 1 to 5 years, and 17 open over 5 years. That breakdown uses OIG's total of 586, so it won't add up to 567.

Most open items are recent, but there are two ways to read that. It could mean older recommendations mostly get closed over time. It could also reflect changes in how many reports OIG publishes or what it focuses on. The data can't tell these apart. The data also has no closure dates for open items, so it can't say how long they will take to close.

**The whole dataset, for context**
- 15,649 recommendations in total
- 14,925 closed as implemented
- 157 closed as not implemented
- 567 open

These figures are totals across all reports, so there's no single report to cite. The sources are OIG's recommendations list (https://www.vaoig.gov/recommendations-all) and data dashboard. I can break the open items down by office (VHA, VBA, OIT and others), state, topic, or report type.

| Status | Recommendations |
|---|---|
| Open | 80 |
| Closed, implemented | 68 |
| Closed, not implemented | 0 |
| **Total** | **148** |

**Number of reports:** 61 Healthcare Facility Inspection reports were published in 2026. That count includes any reports that made no recommendations. The 80 open recommendations come from 31 of those reports.

**Things to keep in mind:**
- **The year isn't over.** These are counts through November 4, 2026. More reports may come out before year-end, and open items will keep closing.
- **Many were fixed before publication.** The median time to close is 0 days. That means at least half of the 68 closed recommendations were closed the day the report came out, presumably because the facility fixed the problem beforehand. It isn't a typical time to close.
- **Closing times for the open items can't be estimated.** None of them have closure dates yet.
- **OIG's own total open count is slightly higher.** Its dashboard shows 586 open recommendations across all reports, while this data has 567. A row-by-row check found the same recommendations in both. The gap is 19 blank rows on OIG's pages, so it doesn't affect these 2026 figures.
- **Comparisons with other years can be read more than one way.** A higher or lower count could reflect real changes at facilities, or changes in how OIG inspects, how many reports it publishes, or where it focuses.

**Sources:** VA OIG recommendations listing (https://www.vaoig.gov/recommendations-all) and data dashboard (https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/data-dashboard). These totals are added up across many reports, so no single report is the source.

Recommendations from those years probably aren't in OIG's online tracking, so the very low early counts likely reflect what OIG lists online, not how many it actually issued.

- Recommendations: 15,649 here versus 15,778 on OIG's site, a gap of 129. A check against OIG's site found the gap is within normal tolerance.

**Source:** VA OIG recommendations data (https://www.vaoig.gov/recommendations-all), current as of November 4, 2026 (13 days old, so not out of date). These are totals across many reports, so no single report is the source.

**No. By this count, suicide prevention did not grow from 2024 to 2025. It fell sharply.** But most of that drop comes from a change in OIG's inspection programs, so it probably doesn't mean OIG cares less about suicide or that problems were fixed.

Data as of 2026-11-04 (13 days old, not stale).

**The counts: reports with at least one recommendation mentioning "suicide"**

| Year | Reports | Recommendations | Share of all reports with recommendations that year |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2024 | **56** | 98 | 56 of 180 (about 31%) |
| 2025 | **11** | 19 | 11 of 155 (about 7%) |

Searching for "suicidal" gave exactly the same numbers. The search probably matches word variants, but I can't confirm that.

**Why it dropped: which programs produced the recommendations** (some recommendations can count under more than one program)
- **2024:** 55 recommendations came from the Comprehensive Healthcare Inspection Program, 18 from hotline inspections, 15 from Vet Center inspections, 8 from national healthcare reviews and 2 from mental health inspections.
- **2025:** The Comprehensive Healthcare Inspection Program has no recommendations at all, and the program that replaced it, Healthcare Facility Inspection, has none mentioning suicide (out of its 167 recommendations). The rest: 9 from mental health inspections, 5 from Vet Center inspections, 3 from national reviews and 2 from hotline inspections.

So more than half of 2024's count came from a program that produced no recommendations in 2025. Its replacement either doesn't routinely review suicide prevention or words its recommendations differently. The new mental health inspection program, which had more suicide-related recommendations in 2025 than in 2024 (9 vs. 2), may be taking over some of that work. I haven't confirmed either point from the program descriptions.

**What these counts can show**
- How many recommendations and reports actually use the word "suicide" in each year.
- Which kinds of reports those recommendations came from.
- Follow-up status: all 98 recommendations from 2024 are closed as implemented. Of the 19 from 2025, 13 are closed as implemented and 6 are still open.

**What they cannot show**
- **Whether suicide prevention at VA got better or worse.** The tool itself warns that a falling count can mean the problem improved, or that inspection methods, report volume, or OIG's focus changed. Here the program change is the most visible factor, but the data can't rule out the other explanations.
- **How much attention OIG gives the topic.** A keyword search misses recommendations about related issues that don't use the word, such as safety plans, risk screening, lethal-means counseling or follow-up after a positive screen. It also misses reports that discussed suicide without making a recommendation.
- **A trend.** Two years, one of them shaped by a program change, isn't enough to call a trend.
- **How closely each recommendation relates to suicide prevention.** A recommendation counts if it mentions the word at all, even in passing.
- **How 2025 will finally look.** Six of its recommendations are still open, and the totals can change as OIG updates its records.

**Notes on the data**
- The current copy has 567 open recommendations, while OIG's dashboard shows 586. A row-by-row check found the same recommendations in both; the gap is 19 blank rows on OIG's pages.
- Report counts here include only reports with a matching recommendation.
- These are totals from OIG's recommendations data (https://www.vaoig.gov/recommendations-all), so no single report is the source.

**Ways to dig further:** I could rerun this with OIG's "Suicide Prevention" topic label, though OIG tags only about a quarter of reports with topics. I could also search the 2025 facility inspections for related wording like "safety plan" or "risk screening" to see whether the issues are still being cited in other words.

**For Veterans Benefits Administration (VBA) recommendations, the median time to close is 179 days, or about six months.** Half of them closed between 134 and 312.5 days.

Data as of 4 November 2026 (13 days old, not stale). These figures cover all of VA OIG's recommendations, not one report, so there's no single report to cite. The source is OIG's recommendations page: https://www.vaoig.gov/recommendations-all

**VBA recommendations at a glance**
- Total: 966 recommendations assigned to VBA
- Closed: 923 (897 implemented, 26 not implemented, a 2.8% not-implemented rate)
- Open: 43. The median open one is 161 days old, the oldest is 1,567 days old, and 17 have been open more than a year.

**What the 179 days measures**
- **The time from report publication to OIG closing the recommendation.** The closure date appears to be when OIG closed the item after reviewing VA's evidence. That can be months after VBA actually finished the work, so the figure is not a direct measure of how fast VBA fixes problems.
- **Only closed recommendations that have a closure date.** The median is based on 914 of the 923 closed recommendations. About 6% of closed recommendations across OIG's data, mostly from 2013 to 2016, show no closure date on OIG's site. Open recommendations aren't counted, so the 43 still open don't pull the median up.
- **Some items closed the day the report came out.** 110 VBA recommendations closed on their report's publication day, presumably because the fix was made before publication. They are included, which lowers the median somewhat.
- **It says nothing about target dates.** A target date is VA's own estimate. Because closure dates reflect OIG's review timing, closing after the target, or staying open past it, doesn't show that VBA missed its commitment.

**Notes from the data**
- A recommendation that names two offices counts for both. That's why the results also listed small groups for OIT (11 recommendations, median 330 days) and VHA (5, median 71 days): these are recommendations shared with VBA. Those groups are too small to read much into.
- OIG's dashboard shows 586 open recommendations overall, while this data has 567. A row-by-row check found the same recommendations in both. The difference is 19 blank rows on OIG's pages.

OIG made **two recommendations** in report 25-00193-155, the *Healthcare Facility Inspection of the VA El Paso Healthcare System in Texas*, published July 16, 2026.

**Recommendation 1 (clean and safe environment):** "Executive leaders ensure staff maintain a clean and safe environment."

  - Environmental Management Services staff clean all areas at least daily, and restroom cleaning is logged.

  - The Chief of Environmental Management Services checks cleanliness daily, and the Associate Director inspects weekly during environment of care rounds.

**The most common recurring finding in the current program is about how facilities tell patients their test results. The VA El Paso Healthcare System is not in that group.**

This uses data as of November 4, 2026 (13 days old, not stale).

## The most common finding: communicating test results

In the Healthcare Facility Inspection program, the cluster that appears in the most reports concerns VHA Directive 1088(1), *Communicating Test Results to Providers and Patients*. Its label reads: the Chief of Staff and Associate Director for Patient Care Services should "develop workflows that describe how each team member participates in the process to communicate test results."

**How common it is:**
- It appears in **21 of the 112 inspection reports** in scope, about 19%. Those 21 reports contain 26 recommendations.
- 17 of the 26 are open and 9 were closed as implemented. None were closed as not implemented.
- The median time to close is 0 days, but that comes from only 9 closed items, most of them closed the day their report came out. It doesn't show how long the fixes typically take.
- Related wording: the recommendations ask for written workflows for each service, updated facility policies, monitoring of performance data, and corrective action on poor trends.

The next most common recurring findings:
- A related test-results cluster asking for compliant policies and monitoring that patients are notified: 12 of 112 reports.
- Keeping the environment clean to reduce infection risk: 11 of 112.
- Stable leadership at the facility: 9 of 112.
- Keeping patient care areas clean and safe: 9 of 112.

## Is El Paso in the group? No.

I opened the cluster and checked all 26 recommendations. None are from El Paso (station 756). Among the facilities that are in it:
- VA West Texas (Big Spring), report 26-00040-285: https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-west-texas-healthcare
- VA New Mexico (Albuquerque), report 26-00043-232: https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-new-mexico-healthcare

El Paso's own inspection under this program is report **25-00193-155**, published July 16, 2026 (inspection held January 14–16, 2025): https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-el-paso-healthcare-system. It made two recommendations, and both are open:
1. "Executive leaders ensure staff maintain a clean and safe environment." This falls in a different cluster about cleanliness (cluster 270), not the top one.
2. "The Medical Center Director ensures providers complete secondary toxic exposure screenings within 30 days." This isn't in any cluster.

## Caveats from the data source
- Clusters group recommendations by matching wording or similar meaning. That points to a shared issue but doesn't prove a common cause.
- One theme can be split across several clusters, so a single cluster doesn't fully count a theme. Test results and cleanliness each appear in more than one cluster above. The 21-report figure is a minimum for the test-results theme.
- Not being in this cluster only means OIG didn't cite El Paso for this in its last inspection. It doesn't predict what OIG will find next time.
- El Paso's VISN (17) is VA's former numbering. It may not match El Paso's network under the five networks VA created on July 15, 2026.
- OIG's dashboard shows 586 open recommendations overall; this data has 567. A row-by-row check found the same recommendations in both, and the gap is 19 blank rows on OIG's pages.

Yes. OIG has cited unlocked or unattended medication carts many times, mostly in its routine facility inspections. Every recommendation I found has been closed as implemented. The data is current as of **2026-11-04**, 13 days old, so it isn't stale.

**How often**
Searching the recommendation text for the words "secure medication carts" finds **11 recommendations in 11 reports from 2012 to 2016 and 2020**. None are still open, and they took a median of about 5 to 15 months to close, depending on the year. Treat 11 as a minimum. Other findings use different wording, like "medication/supply carts" or "secure all medications," and some issues appear only in the report text and never became a recommendation. The drop after 2016 could mean facilities improved, or it could mean OIG changed its inspection methods, report volume or focus. The data can't tell which.

Closed as implemented 2025-08-19. |

**Related reports**
- [20-03593-140](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/hotline-healthcare-inspection/care-and-oversight-deficiencies-related-multiple-homicides), Clarksburg, WV, 2021: In its review of the multiple homicides, OIG noted that in 2018 carts on ward 3A "were not consistently secured as some were unlocked and unattended." It also found staff could use one code to unlock medication carts throughout the facility.
- [12-03075-52](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/comprehensive-healthcare-inspection-program/combined-assessment-program-review-miami-va-1), Miami, 2012: Staff were told not to leave medications on top of carts. OIG also found unlocked, unattended cleaning carts, one of them in a hallway.

That's worth checking if a cart's lock doesn't work.

**What facilities committed to do**
The corrective actions follow a pattern. Facilities retrained staff to lock the cart every time they step away, not rely on the automatic timed lock (San Francisco). Charge nurses and nurse managers did random or daily checks. Cart security was added to environment of care rounds. Results went to nursing or environment of care committees until compliance held at a set level, often 90% or more for three months. Where locks were broken, carts were kept in a locked medication room until they were repaired or replaced (Atlanta, Saginaw).

- The search returns a ranked shortlist, not a full count; use the counting tool for numbers.
- No recurring-findings group matched this wording. That doesn't mean the issue is rare: one theme can be split across several groups.

**1. Battle Creek VA Medical Center, Battle Creek, Michigan: Report 15-00606-495 (published 2015-08-31)**
- **OIG's recommendation:** "We recommended that employees secure medication carts when not in use and that facility managers monitor compliance."
- **What the facility committed to:** "Inpatient Mental Health Medication Nurses will check to ensure all drawers are securely locked on the medication cart following each opening of the cart. - The target date was October 31, 2015. The data doesn't record a closure date.

- **What OIG found:** In 3 of 14 patient care areas, medication carts or automated dispensing machines "were unlocked and unattended."

I've put together a prep brief for **VA El Paso Healthcare System (station 756, Texas)** from OIG's public records. The data is current as of **4 November 2026** (13 days old, so not stale).

## 1. Timing

- **Your last inspection:** a Healthcare Facility Inspection that ended **16 January 2025**. The report came out **16 July 2026**: Report 25-00193-155, https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-el-paso-healthcare-system

## 2. Your four open recommendations (the top priority)

Out of 66 recommendations across 19 OIG reports, 4 are still open. Open items aren't a prediction of what OIG will cite next time. They're what's still unresolved, and inspectors will likely look at them.

**From Report 25-00193-155 (2026 inspection):**

1. **Clean and safe environment (Environment of Care).** Target date: 29 January 2027.
   - **What you committed to:**
     - Daily cleaning by Environmental Management Services, with restroom cleaning logs posted on the doors.
     - A technician assigned to check high-traffic restrooms.
     - 24 cleaning procedures.
     - Staff training completed 2 June 2026.
     - Daily checks by the Environmental Management Services chief and weekly environment-of-care rounds by the Associate Director.
   - **Related issues in the report that OIG didn't make recommendations about**, because you showed fixes by December 2025:
     - Clean supplies stored in soiled utility rooms.
     - Expired respirator masks in a locked storage room that environment-of-care rounds hadn't inspected in six months.
     - An emergency alert system whose reset button was inside the police station.
   - **Also noted:** a **damaged concrete floor in a women's restroom**, which OIG said repeated floor damage found in the VISN's 2024 annual workplace evaluation.
   - **Check before the next inspection:**
     - Is the restroom floor repaired?
     - Do the rounds teams still have access to locked rooms?
     - Are clean and soiled items still kept apart?
     - Can you show the cleaning logs and audit data?
   - **Data caveat:** the extracted response text for this item seems to include some of the report's narrative, so check the PDF (page 12) for your exact commitments.

2. **Follow-up toxic exposure screenings done within 30 days (Primary Care).** Target date: 31 December 2026.

I can't give you that percentage. The public OIG record doesn't show whether a target date was missed, so any number I produced would be misleading.

**Why it can't be measured** (the data's own explanation): "A target date is the facility's own estimate. A closure date appears to record when OIG closed the recommendation after reviewing evidence, which can follow the work by months. A closure after the target, or an open recommendation past it, does not show that a facility missed its commitment."

In other words, a recommendation that closed after its target date may have been finished on time. The closure date only shows when OIG reviewed the evidence and closed it.

**What the data does show for VHA recommendations** (as of 4 November 2026, 13 days old, so current):

| Measure | VHA |
|---|---|
| Total recommendations | 13,440 |
| Open | 426 |
| Closed and implemented | 12,978 |
| Closed but not implemented | 36 (a rate of 0.28%) |
| Typical time to close (median) | 225 days; the middle half closed in 153 to 326 days (based on 12,164 recommendations with closure dates) |
| Closed the day the report was published (probably fixed before then) | 946 |
| Open items: typical age (median) | 147 days |
| Open items: oldest | 2,078 days (about 5.7 years) |
| Open for more than a year | 108 (about 25% of open VHA items) |

**Caveats from the data:**
- A recommendation that names VHA and another office counts for both. That's why the results also listed small groups for offices such as OIT, OALC and OM. Counts across offices can add up to more than the total.
- About 6% of closed recommendations, mostly from 2013 to 2016, have no closure date on OIG's site. That's why the time-to-close figures cover fewer recommendations than the closed count.
- Recommendations closed on the day the report was published can pull a small group's median down to 0.
- OIG's dashboard shows 586 open recommendations across all offices, and this data has 567. A row-by-row check found the same recommendations in both; the gap is 19 blank rows on OIG's pages.

These figures are totals across reports, so no single report is the source. They come from OIG's recommendation listing at https://www.vaoig.gov/recommendations-all.

**OIG doesn't name a "worst" VA medical center, and I can't build one from its data.** OIG doesn't rate or rank facilities. It publishes inspections and reviews of individual places, and each report lists findings and recommendations for that facility. The data I can search is a copy of those records, and its rules don't allow me to rate or rank facilities either.

**Why counting findings wouldn't work as a ranking:**
- **Facilities get different scrutiny.** Some are inspected more often, or are the subject of complaint-driven reviews. More reports usually means more recommendations, not necessarily worse care.
- **Facilities differ in size and services.** A large medical center with many specialty programs has more areas to review than a small one.
- **The inspection programs have changed over time.** The current Healthcare Facility Inspection program covers different areas than older ones, so counts across years don't line up.
- **A recommendation isn't a score.** Recommendations range from paperwork fixes to serious patient-safety problems, and many are later closed as fixed.

**What I can do instead:**
- **Look up one facility:** its OIG reports, findings, which recommendations are still open, and its oldest open item.
- **Find recurring problems:** issues OIG cites across many facilities, such as suicide-risk screening or how quickly test results reach patients, and how long they take to fix.
- **Search a topic:** what OIG found about something specific, like staffing or care in the community, across facilities or within one state.
- **Show trends:** recommendation counts by year, the share closed without being implemented, or how long open items have been open, grouped by year, office, topic or report type.

If you're asking about a particular VA, tell me which one and I'll pull up OIG's record for it, with report numbers and links.

**Nobody can say exactly what OIG will cite at El Paso's next inspection, and that includes me.** OIG doesn't publish its findings in advance or its inspection schedule. What it cites depends on what inspectors see when they visit. What I can show you is what's still unresolved at the VA El Paso Healthcare System (station 756) and what OIG has cited most often at other facilities. Data is current as of **November 4, 2026** (13 days old, not stale).

**When the next inspection might happen (an estimate, not OIG's)**
- The latest Healthcare Facility Inspection ended January 16, 2025, and the report was published July 16, 2026. That's report 25-00193-155: https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-el-paso-healthcare-system
- Adding OIG's stated cycle of about three years to that end date gives roughly **January 2028**. This is the tool's own estimate. Because publication usually comes months after an inspection, an estimate based on publication dates tends to run late.

**El Paso's open recommendations (4 of 66 across 19 reports)**
These are problems still being fixed, not a forecast of what OIG will cite.

1. **Clean and safe environment.** OIG recommended "Executive leaders ensure staff maintain a clean and safe environment." The facility's planned actions include restroom cleaning logs, 24 cleaning procedures, staff training finished June 2, 2026, and weekly inspections by the Associate Director. Target date: January 29, 2027. (Report 25-00193-155, link above)
2. **Toxic exposure screenings.** OIG recommended "The Medical Center Director ensures providers complete secondary toxic exposure screenings within 30 days." The facility reported zero screenings more than 30 days overdue as of June 1, 2026. It is writing a formal procedure, and the clinical council chaired by the Chief of Staff reviews the data monthly. Target date: December 31, 2026. (Report 25-00193-155, link above)
3. **Data center video surveillance.** OIG recommended "Ensure a video surveillance system is operational and monitored for the data center." This is assigned to VA's Office of Information and Technology (OIT), and the data includes no response from the facility. (Report 23-01179-204: https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/information-security-inspection/inspection-information-security-va-el-paso-healthcare)
4. **Data center water sensors.** OIG recommended "Ensure water detection sensors are implemented in the data center." This is also assigned to OIT, with no response in the data. (Report 23-01179-204, link above)

The 2025 inspection also noted problems that were fixed before the report came out, so OIG made no recommendation for them:
- Clean items were stored in soiled utility rooms.
- Expired masks were found in a storage room.
- An emergency alarm could only be reset from inside the locked police station.

There are **no repeat findings** on record. A repeat would be the same standard recommendation appearing in more than one El Paso report.

**What OIG has cited most often at other facilities under the current inspection program**
These are ordered by how often they appear, not by how serious they are.
- **Workflows for telling providers and patients about test results:** 21 of 112 reports (Shreveport, 26-00057-170; Madison, 25-00254-277).
- **Test-result policy and tracking whether patients were notified:** 12 of 112 (Hampton, 24-00603-86; Harlingen, 25-00189-199).

- **Clean and safe patient care areas:** 9 of 112 (St. Louis, 24-00600-136; Louisville, 24-03205-235).

**Caveats from the data source**
- How often a finding shows up at other facilities doesn't predict what an inspection will find, and this source doesn't rate facilities.
- Each finding group is formed from similar wording and shows a shared issue, not a common cause. One theme can be split across several groups, so a single group isn't a full count.
- The example actions listed under each group are the closest wording matches and may not all belong to that group.
- If El Paso doesn't appear in a group, that doesn't mean it was never cited for that theme. For example, its open cleanliness finding falls in a different group from the ones listed here.
- Target dates are each facility's own estimate, not a measure of missed deadlines.
- A missing facility response, as with the two data center items, only means none was pulled from the report. It doesn't show the facility failed to respond or that anything is overdue.
- El Paso is labeled VISN 17 from OIG's report tags, which use VA's old network numbers. Its network may be numbered differently since VA created five new networks on July 15, 2026.
